strengths: Addresses a practically important and challenging task, Video Object Insertion (VOI), with an end-to-end framework combining 4D scene reconstruction, mask propagation, and diffusion-based video generation.
The proposed 4D-aware mask generation pipeline is reasonably motivated and supports user control from only a first-frame placement, which is a practical setting for commercial content creation.

Introducing ROSE++ as an extension of the ROSE object-removal dataset with VLM-retrieved reference object images is a sensible attempt to provide supervision for insertion and photometric effects such as shadows and illumination.

The qualitative results and user study demonstrate strong potential: the method appears to handle several challenging cases (occlusion, object fidelity, first-frame anchoring) and is preferred over Pika-Pro and Kling in the reported user study.
Supplementary material provides some useful implementation details, including Wan2.1-VACE-14B, LoRA rank, iteration count, resolution, frame count, and user-study protocol.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the framework is largely an integration of existing off-the-shelf components (Uni4D-style 4D reconstruction, SEA-RAFT optical flow, SAM2, single-view reconstruction, GPT-4/VLM, DINO, Wan2.1-VACE, LoRA). No new architecture or core algorithm is introduced, and the first-frame-guided video generation idea is similar to prior work. If the intended contribution is Applied/Systems, the evaluation still lacks sufficient systems-level detail and comparison.

Critical technical details of the 4D-aware mask generation are missing or unclear. In particular, it is not specified how occlusion by existing scene objects is handled during point-cloud reprojection, whether depth testing against reconstructed scene geometry is performed, or how the 2D optical flow is accurately lifted to 3D scene flow. The propagation equations and variables are inconsistent (2D flow field vs. per-point 3D motion, centroid update vs. point-wise update), making the method difficult to reproduce or fully assess.

The experimental evaluation is insufficient for the claims. Only Pika-Pro and Kling are used as baselines, despite related work citing several published research methods (e.g., GenProp, VideoAnyDoor, INVI, DreamInsert, AnyV2V, etc.). The abstract and conclusion claim superiority over existing research and commercial models, but no research baselines are evaluated. Commercial tools may also not accept the same mask/reference controls, making the comparison potentially unfair.

The VOIBench evaluation set is small (50 videos, 100 generated outputs) and appears to be introduced without release or detailed statistics. There is no significance testing, and the ablation table shows contradictory trends: the 4D-aware mask configuration has lower CLIP-I and DINO-I than the simpler camera-trajectory masking baseline, despite the paper claiming it improves performance.

Dataset construction and reproducibility are under-specified. ROSE++ dataset size, split, class distribution, and filtering criteria are not reported. The VLM-based object retrieval process is ambiguous (e.g., using GPT-4 for image generation) and may introduce artifacts or bias. Code, dataset, and benchmark availability are not stated.

The paper lacks a limitations or failure-case discussion. Claims such as handling complex occlusions and achieving production-quality insertion are stronger than the evidence supports, especially given the missing details on depth-aware occlusion and the limited baseline set.

Some clarity issues remain: several equations and variable definitions are inconsistent, training losses and the exact conditioning mechanism of the video diffusion model are not fully described in the main paper, and the user study lacks details such as confidence intervals or statistical analysis.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: controllable video object insertion with user-specified placement, temporal consistency, and occlusion/lighting awareness.
The two-stage pipeline is coherent: 4D scene reconstruction, user-interactive placement, scene-flow propagation, geometry-aware mask generation, and diffusion-based video synthesis.
ROSE++ dataset construction is a useful attempt to create insertion supervision by inverting ROSE object removal and using VLM-generated reference images with DINO ranking.
The first-frame inpainting guidance and LoRA fine-tuning on ROSE++ are reasonable design choices for preserving object identity and learning illumination/shadows.
Qualitative examples and user study suggest the full system can produce plausible insertions in some challenging occlusion and lighting cases.
The method builds on strong pretrained components (Uni4D, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, Wan2.1-VACE) and demonstrates a practical engineering integration.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the framework largely composes off-the-shelf modules and prior ideas (e.g., first-frame-guided inpainting similar to [5]), with no core algorithmic advance in 4D reconstruction, mask generation, or diffusion modeling.

Experimental validation is insufficient: the main comparison uses only two commercial black-box tools (Pika-Pro, Kling) and omits recent research methods for video object insertion (e.g., VideoAnyDoor, GenProp, INVI, DreamInsert), despite citing them.

The evaluation lacks ground-truth targets and quantitative geometry/mask metrics. There is no mask IoU, placement error, occlusion accuracy, or 4D consistency metric; subject consistency is measured on masked regions only, and 'Multi-View Consistency' is ill-defined/not clearly a standard VBench metric.

VOIBench is not described in reproducible detail: 50 clips, crawled objects, object pairs, prompts, selection criteria, and target annotations are missing, making the benchmark hard to assess or reproduce.

ROSE++ is built from synthetic ROSE data and VLM-generated object references; the domain gap to real-world VOIBench and potential VLM hallucination / reference mismatch are not analyzed, and the dataset/code is not released.

The 4D-aware mask generation is only qualitatively ablated; scene-flow propagation Eq. (2) is ad hoc and unclear (2D flow lifted to 3D without rigorous formulation), and failure cases under dynamic occlusion or depth ordering are not quantified.

Ablations are mostly in the supplement; the main paper lacks component-wise quantitative analysis and sensitivity studies. The user study uses only 20 participants and 10% of videos, with no significance testing.

Reproducibility is weak: training/inference details are sparse in the main paper, commercial baselines are inaccessible, and prompts, random seeds, and implementation details are insufficient for independent verification.
The paper overclaims 'significantly outperforms existing research and commercial models' without comparing to research models and without robust statistical evidence.
There is no meaningful limitations or societal-impact discussion, especially given applications in advertising/film and the risk of misleading synthetic product placement.

strengths: Targets a challenging and practically important problem—video object insertion with geometric, temporal, and illumination consistency—and presents a coherent system-level solution.

The 4D-aware mask generation pipeline is well motivated: it combines 4D reconstruction, user-controlled object placement, scene-flow-based propagation, camera reprojection, and SAM2 to produce temporally coherent masks that account for camera motion and occlusion.

The ROSE++ dataset construction is a clever and useful contribution: it converts an object-removal dataset into insertion triplets using VLM-generated reference images and DINO-based ranking, addressing the lack of object-reference supervision and reducing copy-and-paste artifacts.

Fine-tuning a strong video diffusion model with LoRA on ROSE++ yields clear qualitative gains in illumination adaptation and shadow generation, supporting the claim that insertion should affect local photometric variations beyond the object mask.

The quantitative comparisons against Pika-Pro and Kling on VOIBench show large improvements in subject consistency and VBench metrics, and the user study strongly favors the proposed method across multiple perceptual criteria.

Ablations are informative: they isolate the benefit of the 4D-aware mask, first-frame inpainting, scene-flow propagation, and ROSE++ fine-tuning, with both qualitative examples and supplementary quantitative tables.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and adequately documents implementation details, training setup, prompts, and user-study questions in the supplementary material.
As an applied/systems and dataset contribution, the work is valuable: it demonstrates a practical VOI framework, introduces a new benchmark, and shows promising production-level insertion quality.
weaknesses: The claim that the method significantly outperforms existing research is not supported by comparisons to academic VOI methods such as GenProp, VideoAnyDoor, DreamInsert, InVi, or AnyV2V; only commercial baselines Pika-Pro and Kling are evaluated.

The commercial baselines are prompt-driven and do not receive the same explicit user mask, placement, or reference conditioning as the proposed method, making the comparison potentially unfair and leaving open how much gain comes from the 4D mask versus unequal conditioning.

Much of the pipeline relies on off-the-shelf models—Uni4D, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, image inpainting, VLM-based retrieval, and Wan2.1-VACE—so the core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental; error propagation and robustness across these modules are not analyzed.

The paper does not quantitatively evaluate the quality of the 4D-aware mask generation itself, e.g., mask IoU, temporal consistency, occlusion correctness, or geometric placement accuracy; only downstream video metrics are reported.

VOIBench is relatively small (50 videos, 100 insertions) and author-constructed, with no clear statement about public release, standard splits, or annotation protocol; the multi-view consistency metric may not directly measure insertion geometry.

ROSE++ is synthetic and derived from ROSE, and the VLM-generated reference images may not faithfully match the true target object; DINO ranking does not guarantee identity preservation, and the domain gap to real videos is not thoroughly analyzed.

The user study is limited to 20 participants and 10% of the test set, and lacks statistical significance testing or inter-annotator agreement; preference percentages alone are not strong evidence for production readiness.

The manuscript lacks a meaningful limitations section and societal-impact discussion, despite potential misuse in advertising, deepfakes, or deceptive video editing; runtime, memory, and trade-offs of the heavy two-stage pipeline are also not discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem in video object insertion by jointly tackling geometric placement and photometric effects, rather than only appearance transfer.

The proposed pipeline is well motivated and comprehensive: it combines 4D scene reconstruction, 3D object lifting, scene-flow-based mask propagation, SAM2 refinement, first-frame anchoring, LoRA fine-tuning, and optics-aware alignment into a coherent system.

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is simple but effective: using an extended mask as a stop-gradient teacher to encourage shadows/reflections beyond the object mask is a sensible idea, and the attention-map visualizations and ablations support its usefulness.

The ROSE++ dataset is a useful contribution for supervised learning of insertion-induced optical effects, and the construction pipeline, including DINO-based rejection sampling for reference images, is reasonably designed.

The experimental validation is extensive, including comparisons with commercial tools, open-source methods, a VACE-based variant conditioned on the proposed mask, progressive ablations, and both general and optics-focused user studies.

Quantitative results show consistent improvements in subject consistency, background preservation, imaging quality, and multi-view consistency, while the user studies indicate clear perceptual gains over strong baselines.
The paper is generally clear, with good qualitative examples and an honest discussion of limitations such as complex physics-aware interactions.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate: the framework heavily relies on off-the-shelf models (Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, VACE) and a relatively simple L2 feature-alignment loss, so the core algorithmic contribution may be viewed as an integration of existing components plus a dataset.

Direct comparisons with recent dedicated video object insertion methods such as VideoAnydoor, DreamInsert, InVi, and Anything in Any Scene are missing, even though these are cited; the evaluation therefore does not fully position the method against the most relevant prior work.

The evaluation metrics are mostly inherited from image/video generation quality benchmarks (CLIP-I, DINO-I, VBench) and do not directly quantify geometric correctness, occlusion handling, or shadow/reflection realism in real-world videos. The optics-specific evaluation is limited to 25 held-out ROSE++ samples, which is a small test split.

The method depends on multiple external modules and an image insertion model for first-frame anchoring; errors from depth estimation, camera pose estimation, 3D lifting, or scene flow could compound. The paper does not analyze failure cases or sensitivity to these upstream errors.

The 4D mask propagation assumes a rigid object and uses KNN scene-flow aggregation around the object centroid, which may fail for non-rigid, deformable, or strongly interacting objects. This limitation is acknowledged only briefly.

The user study is valuable but relatively small (20 participants, 10% of the test set; 30 participants for the optics-focused study), and the benchmark/dataset construction details, licensing, and release status of VOIBench are underdescribed.

Reproducibility is partially addressed in the supplementary material, but the main paper does not state whether code will be released, and reliance on GPT-4-generated reference images and crawled objects raises potential licensing and attribution concerns.

strengths: Tackles an important and practically relevant problem: controllable video object insertion with both geometric placement and optical effects such as shadows/reflections.
The 4D-aware mask propagation pipeline is thoughtfully designed, combining single-frame 3D anchoring, scene-flow-based propagation, and SAM2 refinement to handle camera motion and dynamic occlusions.

Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is a creative training-time idea: an extended-mask teacher with stop-gradient can encourage out-of-mask optical effects while still using only a fine mask at inference.

The construction of ROSE++ addresses a real data bottleneck for supervised learning of insertion-induced optical effects, and the DINO-based rejection sampling is a sensible way to filter generated reference images.
The empirical study is relatively extensive, including quantitative comparisons, ablations, attention visualizations, user studies, and additional qualitative results.
Training and inference details are provided, which improves reproducibility at the implementation level.
weaknesses: The core geometric claim is not directly validated: there are no mask IoU, 3D pose error, or placement-accuracy metrics on real or synthetic data, and no comparison against a strong 2D mask propagation baseline such as SAM2 with a manual first-frame prompt.

The scene-flow propagation is oversimplified: it updates only translation, not object rotation or scale, uses a KNN average that can be corrupted by occluders or non-rigid surfaces, and is not evaluated on support-surface rotations or complex dynamics.

The optics-aware claim is not fully substantiated. The extended mask is derived from source-target frame differences and may entangle object, shadow, reflection, compression, and other changes; reflection effects are not evaluated separately, and optics metrics are reported only on a small held-out ROSE++ split.

Dataset and benchmark details are incomplete: ROSE++ and VOIBench lack release links, licensing, annotation protocols, and clear construction details; 'crawled' objects raise reproducibility and legal concerns.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair: commercial models are given only text prompts while the proposed method and VACE receive masks and/or an edited first frame; some baselines also receive different conditioning, and no statistical significance tests are reported.

The technical novelty is limited relative to the system framing: much of the pipeline is integration of off-the-shelf components such as Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, VACE, LoRA, and OmniPaint, with the main new algorithmic ingredient being the alignment loss.

The evaluation metrics are proxy measures: CLIP-I, DINO-I, and VBench do not directly measure geometric placement accuracy or photometric realism, and first-frame anchoring with an external image insertion model may confound the contribution of the video model.

Some claims are overstated: 'significantly outperforming' is not backed by significance testing, margins are sometimes small, motion smoothness is not best despite the text, and table formatting/labeling is occasionally unclear.

strengths: The paper proposes a complete VOI framework that combines 4D-aware mask propagation with optics-aware video synthesis; the two-stage design is well motivated and addresses real failure modes: object placement under camera motion/occlusion and missing shadows/reflections.

The geometrically grounded mask propagation is a practical contribution: from a single user-specified 3D placement it uses 4D reconstruction, scene-flow KNN aggregation, camera reprojection, and SAM2 refinement to produce temporally coherent masks that follow moving support surfaces and occluders.

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is technically interesting: by aligning fine-mask features to extended-mask features with a stop-gradient teacher, it encourages shadows/reflections beyond the object mask at inference without needing an extended mask.

The construction of ROSE++ is useful for the community, and the paper provides extensive comparisons against commercial and open-source baselines, ablation studies, attention visualizations, and user studies.

Results are strong across subject consistency and VBench metrics, and the ablation isolates the contribution of the 4D mask, first-frame anchoring, LoRA fine-tuning, and alignment loss. Limitations are discussed.
weaknesses: The 4D mask module is a complex pipeline of existing pretrained models (Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, depth/pose models), and the paper does not quantitatively evaluate mask propagation accuracy or robustness; errors from these modules can propagate without analysis.

The optics-aware training relies on ROSE++ source/target pairs derived from a removal benchmark, and the optical evaluation is mainly on a held-out synthetic/simulator split. It is not fully established that the learned shadow/reflection prior generalizes to all real-world optical phenomena, especially complex reflections, caustics, or non-planar surfaces.

Some experimental details and fairness issues remain: commercial baselines use text prompts rather than masks/first-frame conditioning, the VOIBench benchmark is introduced but not described/released in detail, and the user study is relatively small and reported without confidence intervals.

Clarity and reproducibility need improvement: Table 4 right is confusing/inconsistent with the caption, the 'blow mask' typo appears, and reference [1] (GPT-4) is cited as the image editing model for ROSE++ reference generation without sufficient detail, which matters for dataset reproducibility.

First-frame anchoring uses a separate image insertion model and may dominate appearance fidelity, but the paper does not fully isolate how much of the gain comes from the video diffusion model versus the image insertion prior; 'optional' is claimed but not ablated as optional.
Broader societal-impact considerations of realistic video object insertion (e.g., advertising, misinformation, consent) are not discussed.
